agritech-f3f9aaa474.headline: In Panama’s Darién, Indigenous communities test a new way to fund conservation
agritech-f3f9aaa474.fulltext:
- With illegal logging and agricultural expansion closing in on their lands, four Indigenous Wounaan and Emberá-Wounaan villages in Panama’s Darién forest started a biodiversity monitoring project to document their forests’ conservation status.
- Their biodiversity monitoring project recorded more than 200 species across 18,000 hectares (44,500 acres) of threatened forest.
- They’re now using the data as a baseline for joining the biodiversity credits market — a nascent arm of the nature finance industry that’s being touted as a way to help pay for conservation.
- Although biodiversity credit advocates say this market has learned from the mistakes of the carbon credit markets, observers say it’s still too soon to evaluate if it will deliver on its promises.
When Elsa Quiroz saw the spotted body of a jaguar appear on her son’s computer screen, she couldn’t believe her eyes. “I’d only seen them in books,” she said. In late 2025, a camera captured the animal crossing a semi-abandoned path in Puerto Lara, a an Indigenous Wounaan village north of Panama’s Darien forest, close to the Pan-American Highway, an area known for its rich biodiversity. The community was aware of how many birds lived around them, but not of the jaguars.
Samuel Cheucarama, Quiroz’s son, reviews each photo taken by the two cameras installed in Puerto Lara every two weeks. He was as astonished as his mom when he first saw the extent of the biodiversity concealed within Puerto Lara’s forest, which covers an area less than twice the size of New York City’s Central Park. He reels off the list: agoutis, spotted rabbits, turkeys, margays, white-headed monkeys, among others, all found within this wilderness of just 600 hectares, or less than 1,500 acres.
Cheucarama’s work is a small part of a wider project promoting nature-based economic alternatives in four communities managing a combined 18,000 hectares (about 44,500 acres) of tropical forest in eastern Panama. Although the Panamanian government has made efforts to reduce deforestation in Darién National Park, deforestation from illegal logging and agricultural expansion has increasingly been putting communities under pressure, with little to no support from local and national authorities. As a result, communities have been exploring alternatives to make their conservation efforts economically viable. In 2023, they sought funding to assess the economic potential of their forests and started tracking local biodiversity.
Indigenous science and knowledge have guided all stages of the project. So far, they’ve recorded nearly 200 bird species, many of which are found only in healthy, mature forests. In the first year, the cameras recorded 73 animal species, including 15 considered threatened and three “umbrella” species whose protection cascades down to many other species throughout the ecosystem: jaguars (Panthera onca), Baird’s tapirs (Tapirus bairdii), and crested eagles (Morphnus guianensis). The communities are now among the first in Central America using this information to join the emerging biodiversity credits market.
In the last 23 years, the Darién has lost 23,000 hectares (about 56,800 acres) of humid primary forest, according to data from Global Nature Watch (previously known as Global Forest Watch). Many Indigenous communities don’t have legal rights over their lands, so loggers and non-Indigenous farmers encroach on the territories, sometimes backed by the national government, says Muriche Yeucarama, the head of the Puerto Lara community.
For example, in the Arimae community, home to some 170 Indigenous Emberá and Wounaan families, only 8,191 hectares (20,240 acres) of primary forest were legally recognized in 2015, out of 72,000 hectares (about 178,000 acres) the community originally managed, says Elivardo Membache, the community’s president. Today, more than 650,000 hectares (1.6 million acres) of Indigenous territories are still in dispute in Darién.
Scant economic opportunities and the resulting high level of poverty are common denominators across the four communities, according to Franklin Fogoná, a member of the Alto Playón community in charge of biodiversity monitoring.
“There’s no demand for jobs,” he says. The roads needed to take produce like plantains, achiote or cassava to bigger markets are nearly unusable, so they end up selling to middlemen who take a 50% cut, he tells Mongabay over a video call. “There’s not enough money to sustain us,” he said.
“Since there aren’t many economic opportunities, [some Indigenous] people prefer to log or hunt to solve their immediate needs,” says Hayro Cunampio, a member of the Emberá-Wounaan community and coordinator for free, prior, and informed consent at the FSC Indigenous Foundation, which leads the project.
“This proposal stems from the voices of these communities with very specific needs,” he adds. The FSC Indigenous Foundation, he says, talked first with the communities about what they needed, and then looked for grants to help them fulfill their goals.
The project mapped the economic activities in all four villages and developed a plan to improve them. “It opened our minds,” Quiroz says. The information, she adds, has shown her “what do we need to do next, because we need to lay the groundwork for the future.”
Communities take stock of their home
“We have our home, but we never take stock of what’s in it: what exactly do we have in our home, right?” Membache says. “It’s the same with the forest: we have the forest, but we don’t know the wealth or potential it holds.”
From the beginning, communities guided how and where the forest monitoring would take place, says Sabrina Simon, a biologist and ecologist working as the research evaluation lead for Health in Harmony (HiH), one of the partners implementing the project.
They used both bioacoustic monitoring, listening to the sounds of the forest, and camera-trapping, capturing its sights, the latter employing a methodology developed by Savimbo, a biodiversity credits company. Health in Harmony and Savimbo came up with a list of 15 species they wanted to track, including pumas, capuchin monkeys, collared peccaries, and Central American boas. Community members then contributed the local names for these species, and any spiritual, economic, or ecological value they hold for the people, Simon says.
While the list of species didn’t change, the study design did. “We had to redesign it together from scratch, keeping only essential requirements such as the minimal distance between [the monitoring] devices,” Simon tells Mongabay in an email.
Each village picked the members who would set up the devices and decide where to put the cameras, Cheucarama says. “It’s our forest, and we already know it. They don’t know a place they’ve never set foot in,” he says.
Cheucarama wasn’t picked as a tracker, but as one of the two tech experts who would identify the photographed species in their language and upload the location-tagged photos to the citizen science platform iNaturalist, where they would be validated by Health in Harmony biologists and other experts from around the world.
According to Health in Harmony, between 2024 and 2025, 12 people were trained to install 80 audio recorders, which were only in place for two months, and seven cameras that were moved every two weeks. In all, they recorded the calls of 199 bird species, of which 11 were migratory, and 81% can only be found in healthy, mature forests. In the first year, the cameras snapped 73 animal species, including 15 categorized as threatened on the IUCN Red List.
These included the mantled howler monkey (Alouatta palliata), Panamanian white-throated capuchin (Cebus imitator), and great curassow (Crax rubra), all listed as vulnerable to extinction; and the brown-headed spider monkey (Ateles fusciceps), listed as endangered. They also recorded the three umbrella species: jaguars, Baird’s tapirs, and crested eagles.
Even after the end of the monitoring project, Cheucarama says, “we own all the data and devices.”
The photos and recordings have drastically changed attitudes within the community toward their small forested area, Cheucarama adds. “People don’t go hunting anymore. They’re saying, ‘We’re going to put up a “No Hunting” sign.’”
Biodiversity credits, a nascent question
Once monitoring ended, the four Indigenous territories decided to enter the biodiversity credits market with Savimbo, a move that sits outside the FSC Indigenous Foundation project, Health in Harmony representatives tell Mongabay in an email.
Biodiversity credits are an emerging strategy to funnel funds into Indigenous and local communities that protect and restore the world’s biodiversity. Each credit represents a “unit” of habitat restored or preserved, and this quantification is an enticing aspect of them, says Anna Ducros, who researches nature finance mechanisms at the U.K.-based International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED).
In Arimae, one of the four villages involved in the project, the community decided to work with Savimbo because the way they arrived felt different, says Membache, the community leader. At least seven companies had turned up previously “offering millions of dollars” for carbon credits, he says. The community rejected all of them out of concern they would forbid them from using their territories according to their worldview, as has happened in at least one REDD+ project in Panama.
That fear isn’t unfounded: the growing biodiversity credit market is trying to gain traction in the shadow of the carbon credits market, with its successes and many mistakes, Ducros tells Mongabay in a video call. A key learning is to meaningfully engage Indigenous communities from the get-go, she says.
For Savimbo, founded in Colombia and based in the U.S., this has meant giving communities enough time to decide whether they actually want in by first signing a “no-strings attached” monitoring agreement, says Drea Burbank, the company’s CEO, over a video call. For Membache, what convinced them was Savimbo’s transparency about things like the contracts they would sign (all were translated into local languages by local translators and reviewed by the community’s lawyers) and how earnings would be distributed. They also trusted Savimbo because it was co-founded by Fernando Lezama, who identifies as a member of the Pijao people of the Colombian Amazon, who also sits on its advisory board alongside three other Indigenous representatives from the Pijao and Cofán peoples.
If transparency is key to attracting sellers, the quality of the credits is key to attracting buyers, says Richard Field, a professor of biodiversity science at the University of Nottingham in the U.K. and technical co-lead of the measurement working group of the International Advisory Panel on Biodiversity Credits. Savimbo’s methodology of using indicator species as a proxy for forest health, he says, is “probably about as good as you can get” when using camera-trap photos and videos.
Using more sophisticated methods might better capture ecosystem health, but it also costs more and could end up reducing the already small earnings for local communities — a tradeoff that’s a complex balancing act, experts tell Mongabay.
Another trust-building aspect is the third-party certifier’s credibility, Field says. In this case, however, Savimbo looked to work with Cercarbono, a Colombian company that was involved in a highly controversial carbon credit project in the Colombian Amazon. In 2024, Colombia’s Constitutional Court court found that the protocols of the certification led by Cercarbono were too vague to actually ensure a carbon credit project involving Indigenous communities respected collective rights and autonomy. Certification, the court found, was reduced to a “checklist,” and Cercarbono was held liable, along with the project’s developer, validator, and the government.

indian-startups-5291c147be.headline: GalaxEye Secures US Patent for Satellite Imaging Tech
indian-startups-5291c147be.fulltext: In a first for an Indian spacetech startup, GalaxEye has got a US patent for satellite imaging technology, securing its landmark intellectual property that had already been patented in India. The patent covers the core architecture behind the startup’s proprietary OptoSAR technology, which synchronises optical and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) sensors to collect spatially and temporally aligned earth observation data simultaneously from a single satellite over day and night. “This patented technology enables us to serve the global markets and provide weather agnostic imaging capabilities across sectors like defence, agriculture, insurance, disaster response and more,” said GalaxEye founder and CEO Suyash Singh. The grant of the patent comes on the heels of GalaxEye’s successful launch of its OptoSAR satellite Mission Drishti, its first satellite, back in May. Drishti, weighing around 190 kg, is India’s largest privately built earth observation satellite and the world’s first imaging satellite using OptoSAR. However, GalaxEye said it lost communication with Drishti in July after an anomaly linked to a geomagnetic solar storm. It attributed the setback’s root cause to radiation effects from the event that likely impacted a critical onboard system. During its active operating phase over a few weeks, GalaxEye said that Mission Drishti successfully validated critical technologies, operational processes, and infrastructure required to design, build, launch, and operate advanced space systems. The startup is now targeting the launch of two new OptoSAR satellites within the next two years while expanding its in-house capabilities to further strengthen quality, reliability, and execution. Founded in 2021 by Singh, Denil Chawda, Kishan Thakkar, Pranit Mehta, and Rakshit Bhatt, GalaxEye is building multi-sensor earth observation satellites. Last month, it acquired spacecraft engineering company StarOps to deepen its in-house satellite engineering capabilities. It is planning further launches with a target of scaling towards a 30-satellite constellation over the next five years. It claims to have a growing pipeline of domestic and international customers across sectors. The IIT Madras-incubated startup has raised $26.9 Mn in funding to date from investors like Speciale Invest, Mela Ventures, Rainmatter, and Anicut Capital. Most recently, it raised a ₹44 Cr tranche in March as part of its ongoing Series A round, Inc42 learnt. Zooming out, the involvement of private players in the space ecosystem has been deepening over the past few years. Investors, too, are queuing up to back spacetech startups. According to Inc42 data, the funding in the sector surged 94% to $157 Mn in 2025 from $81 Mn in 2024, with the broader market set to cross $77 Bn by 2030.

indian-startups-849d36d66c.headline: ISRO Rules Out Privatisation, Says Spacetech Startups Will Expand Ecosystem
indian-startups-849d36d66c.fulltext: The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) has dismissed concerns that the Centre’s push to expand private participation in the space sector will result in its privatisation or diminish its role. In a statement shared on X, the space agency termed reports and speculation about its future role “baseless and incorrect”. “ISRO will neither be privatised nor will its importance be diminished,” the agency said, adding that it would remain India’s principal institution for advanced space research, technology development, national and strategic missions, space science, exploration, and critical capabilities. The clarification came after key ISRO employee associations wrote to chairman V Narayanan, seeking assurances over the institution’s future role, safeguards for its existing workforce, and the impact of the reforms on recruitment. The concerns followed remarks by IN-SPACe chairman Pawan Goenka that ISRO would eventually stop manufacturing launch vehicles, with such activities being undertaken by private companies or PSUs. Responding to the concerns, ISRO said greater private participation is aimed at expanding the country’s space ecosystem instead of replacing the government agency. “Industry, startups and academia are being enabled to participate across the space value chain, complementing and multiplying ISRO’s capabilities. The reforms should therefore be seen as ecosystem expansion and capability multiplication, not privatisation,” it said. ISRO added that transferring a mature technology does not mean it is withdrawing from the corresponding domain. Instead, such transfers allow industry to undertake large-scale production and commercialisation, while freeing the agency’s scientific and technical workforce to focus on advanced research and complex national missions. Industry To Scale Production Under the proposed division of responsibilities, the production of mature launch vehicles, routine satellites, and other established systems will increasingly be undertaken by private companies or PSUs through competitive processes. ISRO, meanwhile, will focus on frontier R&D, advanced payloads, sensors, propulsion systems, human spaceflight, next-generation launch systems, deep-space and planetary missions, and strategic capabilities. The transition has already begun with the transfer of Small Satellite Launch Vehicle technology to Hindustan Aeronautics. IN-SPACe has also initiated the process of involving private players in the end-to-end realisation, operation, and commercialisation of Launch Vehicle Mark-3. ISRO said the institutional framework established following the space sector reforms gives each entity a distinct role. The Department of Space will provide policy direction, while ISRO will lead advanced research, technology development, and national missions. IN-SPACe will facilitate and authorise the participation of non-government entities, while NewSpace India will commercialise mature technologies and capabilities. Goenka also addressed the concerns on X yesterday, saying a “misleading narrative” had emerged around ISRO’s future role. “Let me say it unequivocally: ISRO’s role is by no means diminishing. It will remain the bedrock of the Indian space sector,” he said. Goenka said industry would increasingly manufacture and scale mature launch vehicles, satellites, and other systems, allowing ISRO to focus on advanced R&D, scientific and strategic missions, new technologies, and complex infrastructure. “The direction is not a smaller ISRO. It is a larger Indian space ecosystem, with ISRO pushing the technological frontier,” he added. Spacetech Startups Take Off The number of Indian spacetech startups has grown from single digits in 2019 to more than 400 by early 2026. These startups are building capabilities across launch vehicles, satellites, propulsion, payloads, ground infrastructure, Earth observation, and space-data services. Skyroot Aerospace emerged as India’s first spacetech unicorn after raising $60 Mn at a valuation of $1.1 Bn in May 2026. Two months later, the Hyderabad-based startup launched Vikram-1, marking India’s first private orbital rocket mission. GalaxEye launched its maiden Mission Drishti in May this year to deploy an OptoSAR satellite combining optical and synthetic aperture radar imaging. However, the startup lost communication with the satellite following an anomaly linked to a geomagnetic storm. Earlier today, Pixxel raised $100 Mn in the largest single investment round for an Indian spacetech company. ISRO said private capital, manufacturing capacity, entrepreneurship, and access to global markets would be essential to increase the size of India’s space economy from around $8.4 Bn currently to $44 Bn by 2033.

india-61fcdb93ab.headline: We have complete trust in our Indian partners: French National Space Agency
india-61fcdb93ab.source: India Latest News: Top National Headlines Today & Breaking News | The Hindu
india-61fcdb93ab.fulltext:
The French space agency Centre National d’Etudes Spatiales (CNES) said that it is not perturbed with the back-to-back failures of Indian Space Research Organisation’s (ISRO)’s workhorse rocket, the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV), and has complete trust in its Indian partner.
The PSLV is scheduled to launch the Indo-French TRISHNA (Thermal Infra-Red Imaging Satellite for High-resolution Natural Resource Assessment) mission next year which is a collaborative endeavor between ISRO and CNES.
“There is always a risk with launches and we know the risks. You must trust your partners and trust is very important in space cooperation because we do difficult things together and to do difficult things you trust each other. ISRO is a huge space player in the world, they know what to do. So we trust them for the launch and the satellite also,” Lionel Suchet, Chief Operating Officer, CNES told The Hindu.
The PSLV had suffered two setbacks. On January 12, 2026, the PSLV-C62 mission carrying the EOS-N1 earth observation satellite failed to finish its intended trajectory after an anomaly was detected during the end of the third stage of the launch vehicle. On May 18, 2025, while ISRO attempted to launch the EOS-09 satellite aboard the PSLV-C61 mission, it couldn’t complete it. It was also due to an anomaly in the third stage of the rocket.
“Setbacks sometimes happen with vehicles and we are not responsible for the launch but we trust our Indian partners ISRO in particular to launch the mission with the vehicle (PSLV),” said Christophe Venet, Director of Europe and International Affairs, CNES.
ISRO and CNES are jointly developing TRISHNA which is engineered to deliver high spatial and high temporal resolution monitoring of earth’s surface temperature, emissivity, and biophysical and radiation variables for surface energy budgeting at regional to global scale.
According to ISRO, this mission addresses critical water and food security challenges, focusing on the impacts of human-induced climate change and efficient water resource management through evapotranspiration monitoring.
The satellite will have two primary payloads, the Thermal Infra-Red (TIR) payload, developed by CNES and the Visible - Near Infra-Red - Short Wave Infra-Red (VNIR-SWIR) payload, developed by ISRO.
“The mission will be launched next year and the French instruments have been delivered to India. They are currently being integrated, we are having regular technical exchanges with our colleagues at ISRO and everything is looking pretty fine as of now,” Mr. Venet said.
(The reporter is in Paris at the invitation of France’s Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs to cover the International Space Summit)

India may introduce merchant fees for payments via UPI
On August 10, India’s parliament passed a bill that would allow banks and payment companies to charge merchants a fee for payments via the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) above a threshold yet to be determined. As Channel NewsAsia reports, this marks a departure from the zero-fee policy for merchant UPI transactions in force since 2020.
UPI is India’s instant payment system for transfers between bank accounts. According to a government study published in February, UPI accounts for 57% of consumer transactions in the country, compared with 38% for cash. In a 2025 report, the International Monetary Fund called UPI the world’s largest instant payment system by transaction volume.
Costs for businesses
India’s Finance Ministry said the fee would be small and significantly lower than charges for card payments. At the same time, business owners and industry representatives fear that even a 0.5% rate would noticeably affect low-margin businesses.
Mahabelly restaurant owner Zachariah Jacob said that around 60% of payments at his three establishments are made via UPI. In some months, the volume of such payments reaches 10 million rupees, so a 0.5% fee would cost his business about 50,000 rupees per month. By his estimate, restaurants retain around 7–8% of revenue as profit.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.
National Restaurant Association of India Vice President Zorawar Kalra believes restaurants could potentially absorb a fee of 0.1–0.2%, but at rates starting from 0.5%, many companies will begin to question whether they can continue doing so.
Threshold and payment model
Large payments are particularly important for merchants selling expensive goods and for distributors. Harsh Bhudolia, co-founder of the Takkada platform, noted that the technological costs of processing a payment of 50,000 rupees generally do not differ from the costs of a 500-rupee transaction, while a percentage-based fee would be 100 times higher.
India’s Finance Ministry said in August that UPI’s rapid growth requires further infrastructure upgrades, stronger cybersecurity, and fraud prevention, and that relying solely on subsidies for the next stage of the system’s development is impossible. According to government data, the number of monthly UPI transactions rose from 6.3 billion in July 2022 to 23.6 billion in July 2026. India spent about 82.7 billion rupees on UPI incentives over the four financial years through March 2025.

world-5422e75d3f.headline: AI cancer cures slowed by chip shortage, says UK's biggest tech boss
world-5422e75d3f.fulltext:
AI cancer cures slowed by chip shortage, says UK's biggest tech boss
- Published
The boss of the biggest UK-headquartered tech firm has said that artifical intelligence will find a cure for cancer that humans cannot in our lifetimes.
Rene Haas, chief executive of Cambridge-based chip designer Arm Holdings, said while modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer was currently "too complex" a problem, computers are "going to solve it" in the future.
Haas also told the BBC that AI would lead to widespread humanoid robots in the next five years, but that its current rapid growth was being held up by a shortage of chips needed to build data centres.
However, he was sceptical about the idea chips could be manufactured in the UK in the future.
Arm designs the brains or CPUs of microchips already used in hundreds of billions of phones, cars, smartwatches and gadgets across the globe.
Earlier this summer, the company's peak share price amid the AI boom made it, in cash terms, the most valuable UK-based company in history.
Haas, who stepped down from the board of British pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca in April, told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast: "AI is going to... find a cure for cancer that today you and I, other humans [could] not in our lifetimes. I believe in our lifetime, AI will help cure cancer.
"Modelling a cell, modelling a human, modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer - it's too complex a problem, not only for humans today, but the computers that run AI.
"However, going forward, as we feed more and more of the models into these computers, and the computers get more sophisticated to run the models, they're going to solve it," said Haas, who also holds a key role in Arm's main owner, the Japan-based Softbank, which has a range of investments in tech including in OpenAI.
Prof Chris Bakal, from the Institute of Cancer Research, London, and CEO of Sentinal4D, said the real question was no longer whether we use AI, it's what we feed it.
He said in labs like his, they are training AI on data generated themselves from patient samples.
"It is not scraped from the internet. It does not need a giant data centre to run. The future of medical AI will not belong to whoever builds the biggest computer. It will belong to whoever has the right measurements.
"That kind of prediction could cut years from the time it takes to develop new treatments. This is where AI delivers real benefit to patients."
Job losses 'overstated'
In a wide-ranging interview, Haas said the chips Arm designs would fuel self-learning AI robots "in a very large way" in manufacturing, cleaning, security, building bridges, and doing repairs within a decade.
"With artificial intelligence, these robots can see, learn, and essentially be reprogrammed for new tasks. So, in the service industry, the robot that was programmed to make a bed can also learn how to arrange the towels in a room, or clean the dustbins, or whatever you want to go off and do."
Addressing concerns that AI would lead to mass job losses, Haas said while there would be some change for workers, "the estimates of jobs going away and being completely replaced by machines is a bit overstated" and outweighed by new opportunities.
He also said fears over a correction in the remarkable rise in the stock market value of AI companies were overstated, because of the long-term demand for AI.
Arm's power-efficient technology was now being used in half of AI data centres worldwide, he said.
This has led to a significant evolution in its business in recent months, selling its own microchips. Facebook-owner Meta asked Arm to develop the Arm AGI chip and "demand has been off the charts", according to Haas, with more than $2bn worth of demand since it was launched in March.
Big Boss Interview: Arm Holdings Rene Haas
The CEO of chip design company Arm tells the BBC AI will help cure cancer, lead to widespread humanoid robots in the next five years, but says its rapid growth is being held up by a shortage of chips needed in data centres.
There have, however, been challenges in the supply of many types of chips, which Haas believes is holding back the roll-out of AI and data centres.
He pointed to plans for massive "multi-gigawatt" data centres in France and the US as well as plans to put them in space.
"We are absolutely in a supply-constrained environment. Can you get enough chips? We need more fabs [chip factories] before we can put a data centre in space."
But he does not believe that manufacturing, currently centralised around Taiwanese giant TSMC, could eventually occur in the UK, despite the government holding talks with the industry about the possibility of bringing parts of the physical chip supply chain over here.
"I don't think it's necessary for the UK to [build] fabs. Fabs are very expensive. They take a lot of specialised workers. They take a lot of natural resources, and there's a pretty broad ecosystem for those."
As the great hope of UK tech for decades, some government ministers have lamented Arm's sale to Japanese investors in 2016 and subsequent partial flotation on New York's Nasdaq rather than in London.
But Haas maintained that half of Arm's employees remain in the UK and said the company was "by far and away the largest employer in Cambridge".

world-745d7538e3.headline: New Panama Canal chief says El Nino could force further transit cuts
world-745d7538e3.fulltext:
New Panama Canal chief says El Nino could force further transit cuts
Daily vessel limit may be lowered to 29 as falling reservoir levels strain key route amid Strait of Hormuz fallback demand
The number of ships sailing through the Panama Canal could be cut further due to drought caused by the El Nino weather pattern, the new administrator of the waterway said on Monday.
Panama has declared a nationwide emergency over El Nino, a phenomenon developing over the Pacific Ocean that is affecting worldwide weather patterns and pushing up global temperatures.
This year’s El Nino is expected to be the strongest since record-keeping began four decades ago.
Panama’s restrictions come even as use of the canal has risen: shippers are seeking an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has blocked in retaliation for the war launched by the United States and Israel.
The interoceanic Panama Canal – which handles 5 per cent of global maritime trade – has already reduced the maximum number of ships allowed through daily, from 36 last month to 32 by mid-September.
It operates using rainwater that collects in two reservoirs, whose levels have dropped due to the onset of El Nino.

world-f219766d03.headline: Europe’s centre fears nationalist wave after AfD victory but only has itself to blame
world-f219766d03.fulltext:
The numbers speak for themselves: Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), a party that dabbles in Nazi imagery, distinguishes between “biological” and “passport” Germans, and is too extreme even for France’s far-right leader Marine Le Pen, nearly doubled its score in Sunday’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt to 43.8% of the vote.
Meanwhile, the centre-right CDU of the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, collapsed to 17.2%, less than half its total in the same race five years ago, and the centre-left SPD – Germany’s other main party of government for the past 60-odd years – scraped 9.3%. The least that can be said is that the centre did not hold.
It is not yet clear whether the AfD, whose local branch in the east German state of Saxony-Anhalt is officially classified by the country’s domestic intelligence service as “confirmed rightwing extremist”, will be able to form a government: it has 39 lawmakers in the 83-member parliament, just short of an outright majority.
But the score is the party’s strongest-ever state result and puts it closer to governing a German state than any far-right party since the second world war. It has sent shock waves round Europe, with nationalists cheering a “historic win” that is “just the beginning” and mainstream leaders warning of a “grave moment” for Europe.
Sweden holds legislative elections next weekend. France faces a crunch presidential ballot next spring. Key parliamentary races will follow there, as well as in Italy, Spain and Poland, later in the year. Far-right parties are polling strongly in all of them, and Europe’s centre fears a continent-wide nationalist wave.
It would be wise not to read too much into one election result in one quite particular German state. Saxony-Anhalt, analysts note, is home to barely 1.8 million voters and has long been a far-right stronghold: in federal and state elections over the past decade, support for the AfD there has consistently been double the national average.
“A far-right party winning a regional election in Germany is not more scary than a far-right party winning a regional election in France, the UK or the Netherlands,” said Tarik Abou-Chadi, a professor of European politics at Oxford University. “Saxony-Anhalt should not be the basis for sweeping conclusions about the electoral sociology of the AfD.”
Nonetheless, the AfD leads in national polls. It is also ahead – although in a far tighter race, with the SPD – in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where state elections are due later this month, and it is lying second even in liberal Berlin. Its rise is part of a decade-long march by far-right parties across Europe.
Almost one in four voters in Europe now cast their ballot for far-right parties, according to research led by Matthijs Rooduijn, a political scientist at the University of Amsterdam, a proportion that has grown nearly fivefold since the mid-1990s and climbed particularly steeply over the past three years.
This analysis, by more than 150 political scientists in 31 countries, found that the proportion of Europeans voting for a far-right party in their country’s most recent national elections had risen in 2026 to more than 23%, from about 10% a decade ago and roughly 5% in 1995.
Far-right populist parties are now in government as part of ruling coalitions in Croatia, Czechia, Italy and Finland, propping up a rightwing minority government in Sweden, and leading in the polls in Austria, Belgium, France and Germany (and, until very recently, the UK).
They have also suffered recent defeats, including in the Netherlands, where Geert Wilders’s Freedom party (PVV) lost nearly a third of its seats to finish second last year, and Hungary, where Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz was comprehensively beaten by his centre-right rival in April.
But the trend seems clear. As Cas Mudde of the University of Georgia, a leading expert on Europe’s far right, put it after Orbán’s defeat: “The far right is here to stay, and many of its parties are as established as the (former) ‘mainstream’ parties. Like other parties, their electoral support fluctuates.”
That steady electoral advance has been achieved despite a refusal by mainstream parties in countries such as France and Germany to collaborate with far-right parties, prompting some commentators to argue that the “cordon sanitaire” or “firewall” has now failed, or even been counterproductive.
By keeping the AfD out, they argue, Germany’s mainstream parties have actually boosted it: the party has been protected from the compromises and failures inherent in government. At the same time, the centre has been “hollowed-out”: forced into uncomfortable, unstable alliances that agree on and – vitally – accomplish little, further frustrating voters and driving support for the extremes.
“There’s a self-reinforcing political dynamic that feeds the AfD’s rise,” said Mujtaba Rahman, of the Eurasia Group risk consultancy. “The weaker the election results, the less common ground in the coalition, the fewer the policy results. The fewer results, the bigger the frustration in the electorate, the bigger the AfD’s share of the vote.”
Many political scientists, however, say blaming the firewall is an excuse, and data suggests far-right parties do not in any case get weaker when they are in government, but become stronger: one recent study of more than 1,300 different governments in 57 countries found far-right parties that entered government averaged a score six percentage points higher come the next election.
Besides the persistent inability of mainstream governments to deliver for disillusioned voters hit by a spiralling cost of living crisis, it is above all the gradual mainstreaming and normalisation of the far right’s ideas that has driven – and continues to drive – its steady advance, political scientists argue.
Research suggests voter attitudes towards core far-right themes such as immigration have not changed significantly over time, but have become much more significant in their voting decisions: normalisation by the media and by mainstream parties that readily embrace far-right framing have legitimised far-right views.
“The entire debate about whether the cordon sanitaire is ‘successful’ or contributes to strengthening the far right completely misses the point,” said Gabriela Greilinger, an Austrian-Hungarian political scientist. “Far-right politics and policies already constantly take centre stage, whether or not the far right is in power. There is no cordon around their ideas.”

other-interests-970d33dc05.headline: Ethical considerations for implantable human brain–computer interfaces
other-interests-970d33dc05.fulltext:
Implanted brain–computer interfaces hold great promise for restoring communication and other functions and for revealing new aspects of human brain physiology. Yet as the number of implantations in humans expands, ethical clarity must keep pace with technical ambition. We propose that this should involve distinguishing research participation from patient care, ensuring long-term support for study participants, ensuring that research participants do not bear disproportionate risks for benefits realized mainly by others, and grounding research in meaningful clinical purpose.

beyond-your-beat-4181412528.headline: Pakistan launch player conduct investigation during dysfunctional England tour
beyond-your-beat-4181412528.fulltext:
Pakistan have launched an investigation into “discipline and conduct” during their highly dysfunctional tour of England, with two players understood to have had their mobile phones confiscated as part of the probe.
A spokesperson for the Pakistan Cricket Board confirmed on Monday that an investigation is currently under way and while no individuals have been named, it follows the removal of seven players from their original touring party last week in response to going 2-0 down with one Test still to play.
The Guardian understands that, as part of this, two players had data from their mobile phones captured by PCB security officials. This is said to have occurred during the aftermath of the team’s 194-run defeat in the second Test at Lord’s.
Amir Mir, the PCB head of communications, wrote on X: “The Pakistan Cricket Board has initiated an internal disciplinary inquiry following media reports concerning discipline and conduct, which are currently being reviewed internally.
“The PCB handles such matters in accordance with its standard procedures. The process is being conducted under PCB regulations, ensuring that all concerned individuals are given due consideration.”
The precise nature of the investigation – ie any potential wrongdoing or otherwise – is not yet clear, nor has a timeline been announced.
So far only Imam-ul-Haq has drawn the public ire of the PCB – and a large section of supporters – after the opener did not bat in either innings of the Lord’s defeat due to a low-grade calf injury suffered on day one.
Speaking in an interview with Geo News last week, Aaqib Javed, Pakistan’s director of high performance, said: “The Imam injury is a big question mark, and a deep disappointment.
“Players in the past used to get injuries, but they used to put on casts and still tried [to play]. We’ll take action against this. How is it possible that a pulled muscle ruled you out of batting in both innings? He should have tried and fought.
“He’ll have to face an inquiry; I can’t say he faked it, but a muscle pull like that cannot stop you from batting altogether.”
Imam has since been released from the squad, along with Mohammad Rizwan, Salman Ali Agha, Ali Usman, Khurram Shahzad and the unused Aamir Jamal and Muhammad Awais Zafar. Sarfraz Ahmed was also stood down as head coach, with New Zealander Mike Hesson moved across from his role with the white-ball team.
Speaking after training at Edgbaston on Monday, Pakistan’s newly arrived bowling coach, Ashley Noffke, said: “I don’t know too much.
“I sit outside that decision-making model above us as coaches. We try to keep the players focused on what they need to worry about.
“I guess that’s one thing I’ve learned about being in Pakistan and coaching for a period of time – nearly 15 months with the white-ball team – there’s always something going on in the background, whether or not it’s in or out of our control – and most of the time it’s out of the players’ control.”
As well as this ongoing investigation, the upheaval has also triggered news of nine players being fined during Pakistan’s recent tour of the Caribbean.
The Guardian understands this was considered a relatively minor issue. The players were supposed to stay within the Player and Match Officials Areas (PMOA) during their warm-up match in Trinidad, only for a group to break away to watch the Fifa World Cup final in a part of the ground not covered by the restrictions.

Indian coal companies are ramping up supply to the coal-fired power plants as coal stocks at dozens of the plants dropped to critically low levels, India’s Ministry of Coal said on Monday.
More than 50 coal-fired power plants in India, where coal is still the single largest electricity generator, saw their coal stocks fall below the critically low level of 25% as electricity demand rises amid the strong El Niño, but supply has been disrupted by monsoon rains.
The number of power plants with critically low coal stocks rose to 53 as of September 5, from 45 on August 26, the latest data by the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) showed.
Coal shipments via rail to power plants have increased in recent days, the Coal Ministry said today. The rise “reflects the sustained efforts of Coal India Limited (CIL), its subsidiaries, SCCL and captive mine operators to ramp up coal supply to the power sector,” the ministry added.
“The number of critical thermal plants (stock below 25% of normative requirement) are being closely monitored, with corrective coal supply measures already in place to further ease the position at these plants,” the ministry noted.
The Ministry of Coal and state-owned Coal India Limited, the world’s biggest coal miner, “remain committed to sustaining this improving trend in rake loading to the power sector and meeting the requirements,” India said.
In August, monsoon-related disruptions to domestic supply tightened the immediate availability and transportation of coal from the coal-rich producing states to the coal-fired power plants.
Stocks at India’s power plants declined by 15.5% between August 1 and 23, as receipts of coal deliveries lagged the rate of coal burns, commodity consultancy BigMint said last month.
The monsoon season in India has been disrupted by El Niño, with hotter-than-usual temperatures driving up power demand.

opportunities-2c327d0b91.fulltext:
The ninth Global Health Exhibition to be held in Riyadh in October
The ninth international Global Health Exhibition will take place in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, from October 26 to 29. The event will be held at the Riyadh Exhibition and Convention Center in Malham. Investors, innovators, researchers, government representatives and healthcare leaders from different countries are expected to participate.
Exhibition program
Participants will be able to explore investment opportunities, establish partnerships, exchange experience and learn about new technologies, solutions and innovations in healthcare. The program also includes sessions, events and specialized working formats.
According to Asharq Al-Awsat, citing the Saudi Press Agency, the eighth Global Health Exhibition in 2025 was held under the patronage of Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Health. Its theme was “Invest in Health.”
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.
Previous year’s figures
The value of agreements concluded during last year’s event exceeded 133 billion Saudi riyals. The number of agreements between private-sector entities increased sixfold compared with previous exhibitions.
The eighth Global Health Exhibition brought together 2,200 brands, 600 speakers among leading representatives of the global medical industry, and more than 130,000 visitors. International attendance increased by 54% compared with previous editions of the event.
